newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Motor racing-Stewart ready for "biggest challenge".
newsitem.headline: Motor racing-Stewart ready for "biggest challenge".

text.p: Jackie Stewart won the world drivers' championship three times between 1969 and 1973 and launched a crusade for safety which was to revolutionise Formula One long before it was considered essential.
He overcame childhood illness and dyslexia at school to become the archetypal modern Grand Prix driver -- fashionable, media-friendly, a friend of royalty, rich, successful and famous.
He was, to many observers, the man who did more for the development of the sport than any other before re-emerging as a globe-trotting marketing man for a string of international "blue-chip" clients.

But now, having launched his own Stewart Grand Prix team with his son Paul, he admits: "I am facing the toughest challenge of my life -- and the first event, in Australia, is going to be the single most important race of my career."

At a time when most men his age are contemplating retirement, Stewart has increased the stress in his pressurised lifestyle by not only launching his own team, but heading it as chairman and overseeing its development.
On Sunday, he knows he faces his first moment of truth when after a winter of testing and development of his team's Ford- powered SF1 cars they take part in the season's opening race.

"From a team point of view, the logistics of having our first ever Grand Prix in Australia increases the challenge. Melbourne is as far away from our Milton Keynes base as we could possibly be asked to travel.

"On the other hand, the Australian Grand Prix has always been superbly organised, the fans enthusiastic and the atmosphere tremendous. It will be one of the most important times in the Stewart family's life."

Since the unveiling of his team's first Grand Prix car in London last December -- more than a month ahead of any of its rivals -- Stewart has made frequent references to his family's support, particularly his son Paul who is managing director of the new team.

Paul, who gave up his own career as a racing driver after limited success, also remains head of the Paul Stewart Racing team which races in junior formulae. It was another venture set up by Jackie Stewart which proved successful -- adding to his reputation as a man with the midas touch.
It is this track record which has added to the pressures on Stewart this time around as he embarks on the massive challenge of Formula One.
"A reputation is built on the past, but success is built on today and the future and that's what we have to deliver.

"Sometimes, I find myself feeling that winning those three world championships seemed very easy by comparison. I wouldn't take anything away from a Schumacher or a Hill, but this has certainly been a greater challenge, more complicated and more difficult than simply being a driver.

"I think even Alain Prost will one day say the same thing. I never promised a win or a championship when I was a racing driver. If we were really good enough, we would win a championship. That is what we now have to do again. But in a much more complicated environment."

Stewart has built his team around the backing of American automotive giants Ford, who are supplying the engines and acting as technical partners. He has secured further financial support from HSBC (the Hong Kong and Shanghai Banking Corporation), Malaysia Tourist Board, Texaco and Sanyo and is reported to have achieved his targets for sponsorship in a sport which requires at least 25 million dollars annually to make a competitive entry.

His driving team is led by Brazilian Rubens Barrichello, 24, who has four years experience of Formula One with Jordan behind him, and rising Danish star Jan Magnussen, 23, once tipped by Stewart as potentially better than the late Ayrton Senna.
The Stewart car was designed by former Arrows designer Alan Jenkins and includes a liberal splash of a bright tartan -- the newly-created Stewart Racing tartan -- in its livery.

"I am a very proud Scot," said Stewart, who has moved home from Switzerland to England to head his new team. "The whole family were born in Scotland. I feel a lot for my wee country. There are only five million of us and our greatest export has always been the people.

"That explains some of my feelings about the tartan. The rest come from my family. Poor Helen, my wife, has been left a lot on her own, but we know it is just the beginning of what I am sure will be a great challenge."
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
